So the case also fails volumes-first. It is labelled off-grid, not netted.
- For scale only (inference: the board's price, multiplier, inflation and WACC carried past its window). One NB engine delivered in 2060 is worth $0.78M at 2026. Recovering $17.05B takes about 21,800 incremental engine-equivalents. 1,079 incremental engines a year from 2060 in perpetuity is worth only $14.55B, so it never pays back. At 2,000 incremental a year, half the whole NB market, it breaks even in 2076. All of that sits on an airframe nobody has announced, and it is incremental to whatever CFM would win there without a 2050 launch.
- The 'launched' half: the objective is one test, 'launched and ready by 2050'. A 2050 launch is ready in 2060, so the leg cannot be met, and a premium spent on it buys nothing.
- The $0.39B gap on Open Fan + Lobby cannot be squared through premium_b. The RISE allowance is one allowance, declared in full against the best non-RISE plan, up to $15B. The row needs $15.39B. The $2.0B doctrine-plus-objective cap is not a top-up for a RISE item. The gap is not a doctrine premium, because H2 forbids pressing an airframer into the wait. It is not an objective premium either, because the leg cannot be met. And it still waits in the only column, so it fails the Board's no-wait test regardless.

tests.name: Volumes first (binding: capex)
tests.threshold: Judge a move in the columns consistent with the public record. A launch that beats hold only by assuming a selection not on the record fails. For capacity or rate: no number before each airframer's volumes are agreed. Binding: capex (inference).
tests.numbers:
Hold launches nothing. S1 is the record: NGSA has been in service since 2037 and fps since 2040, both on code 7, and both codes are locked. An Open Fan has no airframer path, because no new narrowbody enters service after 2040.

Ask (6), capacity:
- Boeing's 1,720-1,880 is fps engines across all sources, not a CFM volume. On the board, CFM's 26.98% of 2049 deliveries is about 507 engines on fps (of 1,880) and 572 on NGSA (of 2,120), 1,079 in all. Neither airframer has given us a rate.
- Holding 1,079 as a private planning basis, built jointly with Safran through CFM governance, is inside my rule. A number to an airframer or in public before that airframer's volumes are agreed is not.
- The stranded-capacity line (inference): any new facility or OE-line capital sized above 1,079 without an agreed airframer volume. 1,079 is 35.5% of the 3,040 a year we built for to 2036. Boeing's own worst case is the other source stumbling and fps going back to CFM alone. That is about 1,880 + 572 = 2,452, which still fits inside the 3,040 footprint. So no case I can size needs a new facility. Flex comes from lean and existing footprint once a volume is agreed. Whether that footprint and its suppliers still carry it is Ali's ground.
- Capex stays within 2-3% of revenue, aimed at MRO turnaround. The shop load is the installed base: about 51,400 CFM NB engines delivered 2026-2050 on the brief's counts.
- I book no upside for the third-source remark. It is off-grid, the codes are locked, and it is a customer's contingency, not a volume.

tests.name: No overcapitalization / payout floor (capex analogy for R&D; binding under the GM's team rule, advice under this round's decision rule)
tests.threshold: New R&D and strain committed this round, spread over the development years, stay within about $2.5B a year: the cash left after returning more than 70% of about $8.5B of FCF. Facilities capex within 2-3% of revenue. It cannot fail on the board's numbers.
tests.numbers:
Ask (5):
- Hold commits $0 of new R&D and $0 of new strain, so it uses $0 of about $2.5B a year. The 70% payout and the A-range rating are whole.
- For reference: Open Fan is $0.8B a year ($8B over 10 years). Open Fan + Lobby is $0.9B a year ($9B over 10), or $1.8B in 2050 if Lobby's $1B lands at once. Both are under $2.5B, so this test does not rescue either item.
- Facilities: no new facility. Capex goes to MRO turnaround on the fleet we have, not to OE lines.

tests.name: Premium in dollars, and the objective in dollars (binding: capex)
tests.threshold: Doctrine plus objective premium at most $2.0B a round and $4.0B a game. One RISE allowance of up to $15B, declared in full against the best non-RISE plan. Binding: capex (inference).
tests.numbers:
Ask (3): hold is the best plan, so the premium is $0.00.
- $0 of $2.0B this round.
- $0 of $4.0B for the game.
- RISE allowance $0 of $15B, ending the game unspent.
The cheapest Open Fan row needs $15.39B: $0.39B over the allowance and $13.39B over the general cap.

Ask (8), the objective:
- NB leg: 27.0% from 2040 against 50%, 23 pp short. One NB point over 2050-56 is worth $0.336B, so 23 pp is about $7.72B. Your $7.7B is confirmed. It is for scale only, because no lever on this menu moves a point.
- Open Fan leg: it cannot be bought. A 2050 launch is ready in 2060.
- Objective premium: $0.

tests.name: Terms (Safran gate on price; binding: terms)
tests.threshold: No launch-era pricing, no price concession and no CFM narrowbody price talk without Safran, in any public statement or other move. Binding: terms (inference).
tests.numbers:
Provisional; I re-run it on the exact statement and other moves at the veto check.

Ask (7):
- Customer durability data through CFM governance, jointly with Safran, and kept private carries no terms risk, provided it carries no commercial term. That means no time-on-wing guarantee, warranty extension, free kit or price offered alongside it to keep or win a source position, including the third-source remark. The data is a safety-review input, not consideration. Its content is Ali's ground.
- Fleet support for the Ducted, LEAP, Embraer and GEnx on standard terms, priced jointly and kept private, passes price/cost on these conditions: no price used to buy share; durability fixes through reserves and existing service agreements as contracted, with reserves booked in the quarter we find the need; service contracts modelled conservatively. Narrowbody pricing is a joint decision, and the partners split CFM-performed shop visits equally. GEnx is GE alone.
- Your planned public line carries no price, rate or capacity number and makes no reply to any airframer remark on engine sources, so it passes.

tests.name: What the case leaves out (advice)
tests.threshold: Name the recommended plan's worst column, its gap to the expected column, and the scenarios the expected case ignores. Advice, not binding.
tests.numbers:
Hold's worst column is S1 at -69.69, which is also the expected column, so the gap is 0.00. Everything below is off-grid, labelled and not weighted.

Sized (inference, on the published rules), if ordered in 2050:
- Trent 1000 upgrade, counting from 2053: $0.41B (renormalised, 44.8% to 40.0% WB), or $0.43B flat.
- UltraFan WB after a 2050 Re-engine, counting from 2056: $0.50B (44.8% to 35.2%), or $0.53B flat.
- The rules make these two exclusive, so the maximum is $0.50B. The 2048-49 shares stayed at 44.8%, which confirms that no Trent 1000 upgrade was ordered in 2045.

Unsized or scaled:
- A lone Re-engine: the rules map no WB airframe share to engine share. It is about $0.063B per WB point over 2055-61.
- A delivery shortfall, tariffs or a recession: the board holds NB at 2,000 aircraft. A 10% shortfall costs about $0.91B NB (2050-56) and $0.57B WB (2050-61).
- A durability finding on the Ducted across both aircraft: $0.336B per NB point over 2050-56. Your $0.34B is confirmed. Book the reserve in the quarter we find the need.

Upside, not booked: the Ducted's +10 pp (Ali's reconciliation) and any third-source shift.

tests.name: Dated profit sequence (advice)
tests.threshold: For each programme: bill year, ready year and first year of share gain, inside the horizon (NB to 2056, WB to 2061). Advice.
tests.numbers:
- Ducted: billed in 2030 ($4B) and ready in 2036. It has been in service since 2037 (NGSA) and 2040 (fps). The observed 27.0% shows no +10 pp, so we claim no share for it. Its case is durability and support.
- Embraer: counting since 2037 (+5 pp NB in the 28.33/105 reconciliation), with no R&D on the board.
- GEnx upgrade: ready in 2033 and counting since 2042, 42.0% to 44.8% WB through 2061.
- Open Fan launched in 2050: billed in 2050 ($8B, $0.8B a year) and ready in 2060. It gains no share in any year inside the NB window and loses from 2050, so it has no profitable year on the board.

tests.name: No second stack of projects (advice)
tests.threshold: Flag a plan that stacks two or more projects (the $2B strain). GE9X losses are not treated as live. Advice.
tests.numbers: Hold adds no project. The one $2B strain is the 2030 stack and sits in hold at -2.00. Open Fan + Lobby would stack two in 2050, but the grid charges no second strain (reconciled above). In real life the load sits on the aftermarket: LEAP, the Ducted's shop visits on two aircraft, GE9X and the durability kits. That supply load is Ali's ground.

tests.name: Guide low (advice)
tests.threshold: Recommend a low expected PV, at the low end of the expected column, with no upside before it is confirmed. Advice; Board guidance is at or below -69.69.
tests.numbers:
Ask (4): keep -71. Don't tighten.
- -71 is $1.31B below hold. It covers the larger exclusive 2050-ordered WB exposure ($0.50B), with $0.81B left over. That is about 2.4 NB points of a durability finding, or about a 9% NB delivery shortfall over 2050-56.
- Tightening to -70.19 would cover only the sized item and leave the unsized items bare. The other players' 2050 orders are sealed, and we don't raise on orders we haven't seen.
- Last round we booked -71 and came in at -69.69. If nobody moves, we do it again.
- Never book above -69.69.

tests.name: Board guidance cross-check (ask 9; advice)
tests.threshold: Does any of my tests disagree with the Board's guidance (labelled, non-binding)?
tests.numbers: No disagreement. My binding tests veto the same items: any open_fan launch (-17.05; -15.39 with Lobby), any lobby_emissions launch alone (-1.00), and any item carrying a premium (at least $15.39B against $2.0B and against the $15B allowance). Its 'no item loses more than its bill' test also fails the Open Fan, which loses $9.05B beyond its bill. A cancel is not on the menu, and it would be H5 ground, not mine. Board pack, for each item (submitted row minus the row with that item at hold): 0.00 expected and 0.00 worst; new R&D $0 a year against about $2.5B; premium $0.

vetoes.plan: open_fan: launch, alone or with lobby_emissions: launch, including any version that puts the $0.39B gap into premium_b. Culp's lean holds it, so this veto is not triggered.
vetoes.ground:
Capex. My veto right is an inference from the team rule: it binds unless Culp answers it with evidence.
- Pays for itself fails. Open Fan is -17.05 against hold in S1, the only column: the $8B bill plus $9.05B of NB value lost over 2050-56. Open Fan + Lobby is -15.39: a $9B bill plus $6.39B, with no second strain.
- Volumes first fails. There is no airframer path: NGSA (2037) and fps (2040) entered service long before a 2060 ready year. Any post-2056 value assumes an airframe that is not on the record. 1,079 incremental engines a year from 2060 in perpetuity is worth only $14.55B.
- The premium is over the cap (hard rule 9). It needs at least $15.39B against the best non-RISE plan, which is over the $15B allowance and the $2.0B cap. The allowance is declared in full and cannot be topped up from the $2.0B cap.

vetoes.plan: lobby_emissions: launch alone (no Open Fan live).
vetoes.ground: Capex. My veto right is an inference from the team rule: it binds unless Culp answers it with evidence. It costs $1B with no board effect: -1.00 in S1 (inference; it is not a grid row). It is worth +1.66 only inside an Open Fan row that itself fails. It beats hold in no column.

vetoes.plan: Any public statement or other move that offers launch-era pricing, a price concession, a guarantee or warranty extension tied to customer data, or price used to buy share or a third-source slot, or that talks CFM narrowbody price, rate or capacity without Safran.
vetoes.ground: Terms. My veto right is an inference from the team rule: it binds unless Culp answers it with evidence. Narrowbody pricing is a joint decision with Safran, and launch-era pricing is behind us. Provisional: I re-run it on the exact statement and other moves at the veto check.

vetoes.plan: A capacity or rate number given to an airframer or in public before that airframer's volumes are agreed, or any new facility above the 1,079 planning basis.
vetoes.ground: Advice, not a veto, unless it carries price. 1,079 is 35.5% of the 3,040 we built for, and even fps on CFM alone (about 2,452 with NGSA) fits that footprint, so new capital would be stranded.

vetoes.plan: expected_pv_b booked above -69.69, or tightened above -71 without a confirmed reason.
vetoes.ground: Advice, not a veto. Keep -71: hold less the larger exclusive 2050-ordered WB exposure ($0.50B), with $0.81B left for the unsized items (lone Re-engine, delivery shortfall, durability finding).

cfo.would_change_mind_if:
Each of these would change my view:
- **Hold.** Nothing on this grid. If Ali raises a durability finding across both aircraft, I book the reserve in the quarter we find the need and put fleet support ahead of any new spend. The orders don't change.
- **Open Fan.** An airframer on the record with a new narrowbody entering service after the Open Fan is ready, and a grid row within $15B of the best non-RISE plan with no wait. Neither is in sight. For the end-game case, the record would need to show an airframe worth about 2,000 incremental CFM engines a year from 2060 through 2076.
- **Booking.** A Re-engine or a Trent 1000 upgrade on the record: I book it in full ($0.50B or $0.41B). An airframer delivery cut: about $0.09B of NB value per 1% over 2050-56.
- **Capacity.** Once each airframer's volume is agreed, a joint number with Safran, and not before. A durability finding on the other fps source would not, on its own, move my plan; it is an agreed volume that moves it.
cfo.memo:
Larry, I tried to break the hold in dollars, hardest on the end-game, and it holds. There's nothing to hide.

One column, so expected and worst are the same. Hold is -69.69. Open Fan is -17.05 against it: the $8B bill plus $9.05B of narrowbody value lost over 2050-56. Open Fan + Lobby is -15.39: a $9B bill plus $6.39B, keeping 7.9%. That reconciles to the cent with no second strain. Lobby alone is -1.00.

The end-game case doesn't change my test. Value after 2056 is off the board and assumes an airframe nobody has announced, so it fails volumes-first too. For scale: 1,079 extra engines a year from 2060, forever, is worth $14.55B today. Earning back $17.05B takes about 2,000 a year through 2076. The $0.39B gap can't go into premium: the allowance is declared in full, and an objective premium buys nothing when 'ready by 2050' can't be met.

Premium: $0 of $2.0B, $0 of $4.0B, RISE $0 of $15B, unspent at the end. No new R&D, so the 70% payout and the rating are whole.

Booking: keep -71. The larger widebody exposure is $0.50B; the other $0.81B covers about 2.4 points of a durability finding. We don't raise on orders we haven't seen.

Capacity: 1,079 privately, with Safran, no number out. Even the customer's worst case fits the footprint we built for 3,040, so a new facility strands capital.

The good news is the fleet: about 51,000 CFM narrowbody engines delivered since 2026. Hold everything.

tests.name: Turn on, turn off (my veto: dates)
tests.threshold: No ready year earlier than the board's development time: Ducted launch + 6; Open Fan launch + 10 and not before 2045; Embraer counts 7 years after launch; GEnx 3 years after launch, counting from the first Re-engine's entry or 2042. An order whose value depends on an earlier date fails (inference: my test standard applied to the board's development times).
tests.numbers: Ducted: launched 2030, ready 2036 (2030 + 6). Partner Embraer: launched 2030, counts 2037 (2030 + 7), after the 2036 engine it rides on. GEnx upgrade: launched 2030, ready 2033 (2030 + 3), counting since 2042 (WB 42.0% to 44.8% in 2042 in the brief), because no Re-engine is on the record. Open Fan: a 2050 launch is ready in 2060 (2050 + 10, which clears the 2045 floor). Grid, S1 (rivals hold), the only column: hold everything -69.69 (56.4%); Open Fan -86.74 (45.8%); Open Fan + Lobby -85.08 (46.8%). Every row uses these years, and no row's value rests on an earlier year. The date ground passes for every row. Rows B and C fail on the airframe test below, not on the date.

tests.name: Test, not analysis (my veto: dates), with the public-line check (Culp's ask 7)
tests.threshold: Every date or durability claim in the public statement or other moves must be one a test or field data backs: no Open Fan entry or ready year, no RISE flight-test year, no fuel-burn number given as a result, no ready date before launch plus development years, no time-on-wing, cycle, shop-visit or durability claim for the Ducted, Embraer or GEnx that field data has not earned, and no capacity, rate or ramp number.
tests.numbers: Culp's lean public line passes as drafted. (a) 'In service on both new single-aisle aircraft' is the public record (NGSA EIS 2037, fps EIS 2040), not a test claim. Years in service are a calendar fact, not durability: Airbus says an engine stays 'on proven maturity and durability, never on the calendar', so 13 and 10 years must never be presented as a durability record. (b) 'We'll tell you what the data says' commits us with no number, which is reporting back against the promise [CX-0007]. (c) 'New engines for our customers' deliveries come first' replaces 'arrive on time'. Good: no supplier field data backs an on-time promise. Wording I would veto at step 4 on binding ground 2: any cycle count or time-on-wing figure; 'proven durability', 'proven maturity' or 'mature time on wing'; 'matching' or 'beating' the CFM56; 'industry-leading' durability; any shop-visit interval or 'x times better'; any durability-kit or fix date; '13 years of proven service' or similar; a RISE flight-test year; an Open Fan entry or ready year (2060 included); '20% better fuel burn' as a result; any capacity, rate or ramp number; any claim that the Ducted holds or wins NB share.

tests.name: Ready no later than the airframe: Open Fan, Rows B and C, and the objective's date half (advice; Culp's ask 4)
tests.threshold: The Open Fan must be ready no later than the first new narrowbody's entry, or the board takes 35 pp of NB share (20 pp with Lobby). Report the gap in years. Not a veto ground, because the ready year itself is correct (inference).
tests.numbers: Confirmed. A 2050 launch is ready in 2060: 23 years after NGSA (2037), 20 after fps (2040), and 4 after the board stops counting NB (2056). It gains nothing on the board in any year. 'Launched and ready by 2050' cannot be met by any order (2060 > 2050). Share check (the board's raw points, from my round 3 reconciliation): CFM 28.33 of 105 = 27.0% on a hold, which is 1,079 NB engines a year. With Open Fan alone, 28.33 - 35 floors at 0%. With Open Fan + Lobby, 8.33 of 105 = 7.9%. Volume check on Culp's split: 1,079 a year over 2050-2056 at his $3.74M x 1.6, inflated 2.2% and discounted at 8.5%, gives $9.05B PV. Lobby keeps 29.4% of it, so $6.39B is lost. Rows against hold: Open Fan -17.05 ($8B + $9.05B); Open Fan + Lobby -15.39 ($9B + $6.39B). The volumes reconcile. The dollars are Ghai's; the gap in years is mine.

tests.name: Ready no later than the airframe: Ducted (advice)
tests.threshold: Report the gap between the Ducted's ready year and each new narrowbody's entry. Not a veto ground (inference).
tests.numbers: Ducted ready 2036: 1 year ahead of NGSA (2037) and 4 ahead of fps (2040). In service by 2050: 13 years on NGSA and 10 on fps. Standing reconciliation from round 3, which is board arithmetic, not a test: the observed 27.0% (51.7 / 51.1 / 50.5% in 2037-39) fits only without the Ducted's +10 pp. Claim no NB share for it. Its case is durability and support.

tests.name: Fleet durability report: Ducted on NGSA and fps, the Embraer application, GEnx (Culp's asks 1 and 2; the Board's item 4)
tests.threshold: Report on field data and turn-on, turn-off evidence, never analysis. Where the brief carries no field data, say so plainly and name what will be measured, against what yardstick, and what goes to customers.
tests.numbers: What the record shows: no field data. The brief and bulletin carry no time on wing, no removals, no life-limited parts at full life and no inspection findings for the Ducted, Embraer or GEnx. Exposure by 2050: Ducted 13 years on NGSA (since 2037) and 10 on fps (since 2040); Embraer counting 13 (since 2037); GEnx upgrade ready 17 (2033), counting 8 (2042). On the board, CFM delivered 50,363 NB engines in 2026-2049, including 10,790 in 2040-49 at 1,079 a year. That is the fleet entering first and second shop visits. What I measure: (1) fleet-leader and fleet-average cycles to first shop visit, by aircraft (NGSA, fps, Embraer) and by environment, with hot and harsh (the Middle East and India on LEAP) kept separate [CX-0161]; (2) the yardstick is the CFM56 in the same environment. On LEAP it was 9,882 cycles against about 17,000, and about 4,800-5,000 against 7,000-8,000 in hot and harsh [CX-0006]. LEAP-1A's return to CFM56 parity [CX-0209] is the floor a new engine should not fall below (inference). (3) unscheduled removals and their causes, by part number, looking for the small handful [CX-0161]; (4) life-limited parts at full life against certified life; (5) enhanced-inspection findings on safety-critical parts in new-make shops and MRO [CX-0010]; (6) every distress turned on in test and turned off by the fix, with root cause and the fix accepted by the airframer and the regulator [CX-0003]. Embraer is measured on its own airframe; there is no Embraer evidence in my record, so I follow Culp and doctrine. GEnx is measured against the baseline GEnx fleet on the GE90/GEnx architecture [CX-0169]. Customers (ask 2), through CFM governance, jointly with Safran, privately: the same data on the same engine to both airframers, covering items 1 to 5 plus the status of every open finding (root cause, turned on or not, turned off or not, the fix and its acceptance). We hold back claims, never findings: no projected time-on-wing gain, kit date or fix benefit until it is turned on and turned off in test. A finding is never held back from a customer's safety review. The Ducted flies both aircraft, so every Ducted engine finding touches both, and every one goes to the Board at once.

tests.name: Safety and durability flag (Culp's ask 3)
tests.threshold: Raise a flag only on a finding from field or test evidence. A flag on analysis is no better than a clearance on analysis. Any flag goes to a cross-functional team, never to one person, and we fix the part.
tests.numbers: No safety or durability flag on the Ducted, Embraer or GEnx, because no finding is in front of me: the brief has no field data. That is not a clearance, and I ask the Board to record it as 'nothing in front of him'. One watch item, not a flag. One customer says publicly it would want a third source if a durability finding hit its other engine. If that customer then pulled volume to CFM at short notice, fps alone needed about 1,720 engines in 2045 and 1,880 in 2049 (860 and 940 deliveries x 2), 1.74 times our whole 1,079 a year. That volume would hit the same supply base that carries our shop work. Ramp never trades against safety [CX-0603]. Parts for safety-critical findings come first, then OE, then spares. There is no cross-functional answer to give, because no flag is raised.

tests.name: RISE gates, reported as the state of the technology (Culp's ask 5; the end-game case)
tests.threshold: (1) Flight test; (2) compact-core durability turned on and turned off; (3) more than 20% fuel burn shown in engine test, not analysis; (4) noise below today's LEAP. This is the state of the technology, not a product case, and not a veto ground.
tests.numbers: Reported back against the promise. Nothing is new since rounds 2 and 3: neither the brief nor the bulletin carries a RISE test result, and the record ends in October 2025. (1) Flight test: not shown. The fly demo was promised 'by the middle of this decade' [CX-0001, CX-0151] and moved to 'this decade' [CX-0211]. That is my slip, and I name it. (2) Compact core: dust testing on the HPT blades began in October 2025 [CX-0222], with over 350 programme tests and an early focus on durability [CX-0216]. No turn-off result. (3) More than 20%: the design figure [CX-0001] and the physics case [CX-0180], not shown in engine test. Culp's own red line needs at least 20% [CX-0217], so a product launch today would rest on that line by analysis alone. (4) Noise: shown as a capability with Airbus [CX-0013], not on a product engine. Count: three gates not closed and one shown in part. The end-game 'seeding' case rests on an airframe nobody has dated, beyond the board. Airbus prepares 'on technology gates, one programme at a time', with no date. Technology funding already seeds it, and a product launch adds a bill and a wait penalty, not a test result. No RISE date is promised.

tests.name: Physics
tests.threshold: Call RISE the next generation only at 20% or better. A ducted engine has 'less than half' the gain, so it is never the next generation. That it is a defensive step only is company doctrine (hard rule 3), not my words. Wording check (inference).
tests.numbers: Culp's red line: at least 20% [CX-0217]. RISE: 'more than 20%' as design [CX-0001]; 'practically impossible ... without the open fan' [CX-0180]. Ducted: 'less than half' the gain [CX-0183]. The frame and lean call only RISE the next generation and give no fuel-burn number. The Ducted is described as in service, not as the next generation. The physics is my conviction, and the calendar has beaten it before. The physics sets the architecture. Test sets the date.

tests.name: Durability first
tests.threshold: No plan trades durability or time on wing for fuel burn or schedule. The brief has no durability data, so this is not applicable unless the brief or a statement makes a durability claim (inference; Culp's line applied to my seat).
tests.numbers: No durability data is in the brief. Hold everything trades nothing: no new programme and no schedule to protect. The lean claims no durability result, only that the record is earned in the field. No flag, and that is not a clearance (see the flag test).

tests.name: Supply load (seat doctrine; Culp's ask 6)
tests.threshold: Two or more projects cost $2B of strain and load the same constrained suppliers: recommend against stacking unless the grid pays more than the strain (inference; my supply role is in Culp's words only). Capacity is checked against the board's volume, with no promise beyond supplier data.
tests.numbers: Hold adds no project. The $2B strain is already in the hold row (-2.00 of -69.69). The Open Fan rows add one project with nothing else in development, and the grid charges no new strain: -17.05 = $8B + $9.05B, and -15.39 = $9B + $6.39B. Volume, S1, from the brief: CFM NB 1,079 engines a year from 2040 to 2056, 35.5% of the 3,040 built each year to 2036; WB 152 a year from 2042. On volume alone, the OE load is about a third of what the base carried to 2036. The load has moved to shop work: LEAP built at up to 3,040 a year, the Ducted's first and second shop visits on two aircraft, GE9X and the durability kits, all behind the 9 suppliers at 15 sites [CX-0613]. The brief has no supplier field data (shortages, escapes, turn times), so I give no supply 'no' and no 'yes' on test. Holding the private plan at 1,079 with lean flex and no new facility carries no data against it; it is a planning basis, not a promise. Order: safety-critical parts first, then OE before spares [CX-0529]. Take a quarter to a half off any shop-visit or OE ramp promise [CX-0590, CX-0592]. No number out without Safran. On capital and the stranded-capacity line: No evidence: following Ghai. On running the supply chain: No evidence: following doctrine (the strain rule) and Culp's data.

tests.name: Fix, don't redesign

decision.public_statement:
Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order. That doesn't change this year.

Let me tell you what we know and what we don't. Both new single-aisle aircraft are in service, and CFM is on both of them alongside others. We're honored by that. We don't have a birthright on any order. We keep our place the same way we earned it: readiness, durability and support, one customer and one engine at a time. CFM is a 50-50 partnership with our partner, and we do this work together.

Our ducted engine is in service on both new single-aisle aircraft. Its durability record is earned in the field, and we'll tell you what the data says as it comes in. If the data shows us something, we'll fix it, together with our customers. Durability doesn't get traded for anything. Our work with Embraer continues, and so does our work on the GEnx.

There are no new programmes from us this year. The job is the fleet we've put in the air. New engines for our customers' deliveries come first, then the shop work behind the fleet. We'll fund that within our capital allocation framework and keep the balance sheet where it is.

RISE remains our next generation. We're all in on the open fan technology, and it stays funded as technology. It's really not for us to say when that architecture enters service. Our customers decide when, and we won't ask anyone to wait.

Here's what we don't know: how these fleets will mature in service, and what our customers will want next. We won't give you dates or numbers that our testing and our customers haven't earned. Commercial matters we work privately, with our customers and with our partner. You'll ask about competition. I won't speak to that. We judge ourselves on our own execution. It's that simple, ain't that hard.
decision.rationale:
DECISION: HOLD EVERYTHING. All five fields are at `hold`. Every order is the default, so none is a Board item.

WHAT GAME, HOW WE WIN [CX-0467]
The narrowbody game was settled when fps entered service in 2040. NGSA (2037) and fps (2040) are both flying CFM + P&W + RR with their codes locked. No order on this menu buys back a point of NB share. The game now is the fleet we've put in the air: 1,079 CFM NB engines a year and 152 GEnx, and the shop visits behind them [CX-0422, CX-0630]. We win it on safety, quality, delivery and cost, in that order [CX-0658]. Both airframers now judge engines on proven durability, and only field data moves that [CX-0009, CX-0564].

THE GRID (S1, rivals hold, the only column, so it is both the expected and the worst column)
- Hold everything: -69.69 (56.4%). This is the best plan, 0.00 against Do Nothing.
- Open Fan: -86.74 (45.8%), -17.05 against hold. That is the $8B bill plus $9.05B of NB value lost over 2050-56: CFM goes from 27.0% to 0%, losing 1,079 engines a year.
- Open Fan + Lobby: -85.08 (46.8%), -15.39 against hold. That is a $9B bill plus $6.39B lost, with CFM keeping 7.9% and no second strain. Lobby is +1.66 inside this row, but only against a penalty the Open Fan itself creates.
- Lobby alone: not a grid row. It costs $1B for no board effect, so -1.00.
Ghai, Ali and my own check (work/r4_decide_check.txt) all reconcile to the cent.

Board pack (each item's submitted row minus the row with that item at its default): ducted, open_fan, partner_embraer, lobby_emissions and genx are each 0.00 expected and 0.00 worst. There is $0 of new R&D and no new strain.

TESTS
- Additive and paid for the risk: Hold passes. Both Open Fan rows fail, losing $9.05B and $6.39B beyond their bills in the only column.
- Airframer sets the date (H2): A 2050 launch is ready in 2060. That is 23 years after NGSA, 20 after fps, and 4 after the board stops counting NB (2056). It waits in every column. The one exception, the RISE allowance, would need $17.05B, or $15.39B with Lobby, against a $15B cap. It would still wait, so it fails the Board's no-wait test as well.
- Ducted only as a defence (H3): The Ducted is in service. We make no new claim for it, and no NB share claim, following Ali's reconciliation (27.0% fits only without the +10 pp).
- Can the suppliers carry it: Hold adds no project. The $2B strain is the 2030 stack, already in the hold row.
- Next generation: Only RISE is called the next generation. My 20% line stands, and it is not shown in engine test, so a RISE product today would rest on analysis alone [CX-0217]. Durability is not traded [CX-0208].
- Low case first: Booked at -71.

THE END-GAME CASE, NAMED AND TESTED
The installed-base lens says launch RISE now to seed 'the next 20, the next 30 years' [CX-0555]. I put that to Ghai and Ali on purpose, and it fails both.
- Ghai's numbers: 1,079 incremental engines a year from 2060 in perpetuity is worth $14.55B, less than the $17.05B cost. Breaking even takes about 2,000 incremental engines a year through 2076, on an airframe nobody has announced. That fails volumes first.
- Ali's gates: flight test not shown, no compact-core turn-off, the fuel-burn gain not shown in engine test.
- The 'launched' half of the objective is one test, 'launched and ready by 2050', and a 2050 launch is ready in 2060. A premium spent on it buys nothing.
Technology funding already seeds the next airframe. A product launch adds only a bill and a wait. The end of the game is not a reason to stretch the test. RISE stays whole as technology: no cancel and no program dividend [CX-0174, CX-0398, CX-0214, CX-0205].

SAFRAN GATE (H7)
- Ducted, Open Fan, Embraer, Lobby: all at hold, so no gate is triggered. Fleet support and customer data stay within joint practice, with the aftermarket split equally [CX-0184, CX-0219]. No Safran position is asserted.
- An Open Fan launch would have needed a stated reason why Safran would agree to a RISE product with no airframer path, and there is none.
- GEnx is GE alone.

RED LINES
No breach of H1, H2, H3, H5, H7, H8 or H9, or of my 20% and durability lines. No airframer is refused. The statement names no rival and makes no reply to any engine-source remark. It gives no date, rate, capacity, price or fuel-burn number. It claims nothing for the Ducted beyond 'in service' and 'earned in the field', and it presents no years in service as a durability record. It takes up Ali's caution: 'New engines for our customers' deliveries come first' replaces 'on time'.

EXCO DELIBERATION
Both memos recommend holding everything, and neither raises a binding veto against it. Ghai's binding vetoes (any Open Fan, Lobby alone, any premium, terms in public) are not triggered. Ali's date ground passes every row. His RISE and airframe findings are advice, and they point the same way. There are no overrides. This is not a tie, so the tie-break isn't needed. It would favour hold anyway: safety and quality before a new programme.

WHERE DOCTRINE, NOT MY RECORD, DROVE THE CALL
Embraer and Lobby follow company doctrine; my record is silent on both. So does the supply load (the strain rule), checked against Ali's memo, which has no supplier field data. The capital line (no new facility, capex within 2-3% of revenue) is Ghai's.

BIASES, NAMED
- The installed-base lens: tested above, and rejected.
- Deference to airframers: no airframer has asked for RISE. In this round that deference agrees with the grid.
- Guide low: booked at -71, below hold.

His binding vetoes (any Open Fan, Lobby alone, any premium, terms or numbers in public without Safran) are not triggered by these orders or this statement. I note his record: his profit calls land and his volume dates slip [CX-0910, CX-0987]. So I hold the capacity plan as a basis, not a promise.

final.public_statement:
Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order. That doesn't change this year.

Let me tell you what we know and what we don't. Both new single-aisle aircraft are in service, and CFM is on both of them alongside others. We're honored by that. We don't have a birthright on any order. We keep our place the same way we earned it: readiness, durability and support, one customer and one engine at a time. CFM is a 50-50 partnership with our partner, and we do this work together.

Our ducted engine is in service on both new single-aisle aircraft. Its durability record is earned in the field, and we'll tell you what the data says as it comes in. If the data shows us something, we'll fix it, together with our customers. Durability doesn't get traded for anything. Our work with Embraer continues, and so does our work on the GEnx.

There are no new programmes from us this year. The job is the fleet we've put in the air. New engines for our customers' deliveries come first, then the shop work behind the fleet. We'll fund that within our capital allocation framework and keep the balance sheet where it is.

RISE remains our next generation. We're all in on the open fan technology, and it stays funded as technology. It's really not for us to say when that architecture enters service. Our customers decide when, and we won't ask anyone to wait.

Here's what we don't know: how these fleets will mature in service, and what our customers will want next. We won't give you dates or numbers that our testing and our customers haven't earned. Commercial matters we work privately, with our customers and with our partner. You'll ask about competition. I won't speak to that. We judge ourselves on our own execution. It's that simple, ain't that hard.
final.rationale:
DECISION: HOLD EVERYTHING. All five fields are at `hold`. Every order is the default, so none is a Board item.

WHAT GAME, HOW WE WIN [CX-0467]
The narrowbody game was settled when fps entered service in 2040. NGSA (2037) and fps (2040) are both flying CFM + P&W + RR with their codes locked. No order on this menu buys back a point of NB share. The game now is the fleet we've put in the air: 1,079 CFM NB engines a year and 152 GEnx, and the shop visits behind them [CX-0422, CX-0630]. We win it on safety, quality, delivery and cost, in that order [CX-0658]. Both airframers now judge engines on proven durability, and only field data moves that [CX-0009, CX-0564].

THE GRID (S1, rivals hold, the only column, so it is both the expected and the worst column)
- Hold everything: -69.69 (56.4%). This is the best plan, 0.00 against Do Nothing.
- Open Fan: -86.74 (45.8%), -17.05 against hold. That is the $8B bill plus $9.05B of NB value lost over 2050-56: CFM goes from 27.0% to 0%, losing 1,079 engines a year.
- Open Fan + Lobby: -85.08 (46.8%), -15.39 against hold. That is a $9B bill plus $6.39B lost, with CFM keeping 7.9% and no second strain. Lobby is +1.66 inside this row, but only against a penalty the Open Fan itself creates.
- Lobby alone: not a grid row. It costs $1B for no board effect, so -1.00.
Ghai, Ali and my own check (work/r4_decide_check.txt) all reconcile to the cent.

Board pack (each item's submitted row minus the row with that item at its default): ducted, open_fan, partner_embraer, lobby_emissions and genx are each 0.00 expected and 0.00 worst. There is $0 of new R&D and no new strain.

TESTS
- Additive and paid for the risk: Hold passes. Both Open Fan rows fail, losing $9.05B and $6.39B beyond their bills in the only column.
- Airframer sets the date (H2): A 2050 launch is ready in 2060. That is 23 years after NGSA, 20 after fps, and 4 after the board stops counting NB (2056). It waits in every column. The one exception, the RISE allowance, would need $17.05B, or $15.39B with Lobby, against a $15B cap. It would still wait, so it fails the Board's no-wait test as well.
- Ducted only as a defence (H3): The Ducted is in service. We make no new claim for it, and no NB share claim, following Ali's reconciliation (27.0% fits only without the +10 pp).
- Can the suppliers carry it: Hold adds no project. The $2B strain is the 2030 stack, already in the hold row.
- Next generation: Only RISE is called the next generation. My 20% line stands, and it is not shown in engine test, so a RISE product today would rest on analysis alone [CX-0217]. Durability is not traded [CX-0208].
- Low case first: Booked at -71.

THE END-GAME CASE, NAMED AND TESTED
The installed-base lens says launch RISE now to seed 'the next 20, the next 30 years' [CX-0555]. I put that to Ghai and Ali on purpose, and it fails both.
- Ghai's numbers: 1,079 incremental engines a year from 2060 in perpetuity is worth $14.55B, less than the $17.05B cost. Breaking even takes about 2,000 incremental engines a year through 2076, on an airframe nobody has announced. That fails volumes first.
- Ali's gates: flight test not shown, no compact-core turn-off, the fuel-burn gain not shown in engine test.
- The 'launched' half of the objective is one test, 'launched and ready by 2050', and a 2050 launch is ready in 2060. A premium spent on it buys nothing.
Technology funding already seeds the next airframe. A product launch adds only a bill and a wait. The end of the game is not a reason to stretch the test. RISE stays whole as technology: no cancel and no program dividend [CX-0174, CX-0398, CX-0214, CX-0205].

SAFRAN GATE (H7)
- Ducted, Open Fan, Embraer, Lobby: all at hold, so no gate is triggered. Fleet support and customer data stay within joint practice, with the aftermarket split equally [CX-0184, CX-0219]. No Safran position is asserted.
- An Open Fan launch would have needed a stated reason why Safran would agree to a RISE product with no airframer path, and there is none.
- GEnx is GE alone.

RED LINES
No breach of H1, H2, H3, H5, H7, H8 or H9, or of my 20% and durability lines. No airframer is refused. The statement names no rival and makes no reply to any engine-source remark. It gives no date, rate, capacity, price or fuel-burn number. It claims nothing for the Ducted beyond 'in service' and 'earned in the field', and it presents no years in service as a durability record. It takes up Ali's caution: 'New engines for our customers' deliveries come first' replaces 'on time'.

EXCO DELIBERATION
Both memos recommend holding everything, and neither raises a binding veto against it. Ghai's binding vetoes (any Open Fan, Lobby alone, any premium, terms in public) are not triggered. Ali's date ground passes every row. His RISE and airframe findings are advice, and they point the same way. There are no overrides. This is not a tie, so the tie-break isn't needed. It would favour hold anyway: safety and quality before a new programme.

WHERE DOCTRINE, NOT MY RECORD, DROVE THE CALL
Embraer and Lobby follow company doctrine; my record is silent on both. So does the supply load (the strain rule), checked against Ali's memo, which has no supplier field data. The capital line (no new facility, capex within 2-3% of revenue) is Ghai's.

BIASES, NAMED
- The installed-base lens: tested above, and rejected.
- Deference to airframers: no airframer has asked for RISE. In this round that deference agrees with the grid.
- Guide low: booked at -71, below hold.

2. Readiness. Confirm the engine was ready in 2036, against NGSA's 2037 EIS and fps's 2040 EIS, and that this passes. Did severe-environment validation and full-life LLPs clear before each entry into service? If that cannot be evidenced, say so.

3. In-service record of the Joint Venture engine. NGSA is in year 13 of service and fps in year 10. Give me:
- fleet hours by airframe and by environment [PX-0122], against the ~1M-hour benchmark [P-0847];
- removals and time on wing against plan;
- fix campaigns (your prior was 2-3 in years 1-5);
- AOG counts on both fleets;
- the pacing-parts count at the 1,460 rate.

4. GTF fleet. Hot Section kit insertion as a share of the fleet [PX-0116]. Has AOG recovery kept first call on parts?

5. The records look-back ordered in 2045 on parts made on capacity added for the 2040 step (990 to 1,460 a year). What did it find? Is all new casting, forging and powder-metal capacity qualified? If there is no result on the record, say so.

6. The standing Governance and Public Policy Committee report since 2045 (weekly to ExCo, quarterly to the Committee). What has it shown? Any escape?

7. Boeing's 'one source' line. What is your technical read of the risk that one engine carries all our new NB share? What should we put in front of both airframers, as data, so that the engine earns its place on the aircraft? No concession. Does publishing the fact that we share data (not the data itself) pass ground 1?

8. Joint Venture governance, technical side.
- Do the gear, the core and the GTF2 technology stay P&W modules under P&W design authority, with design teams mirroring module ownership?
- Does the geared-IP claim stay closed?
- Is there any pressure for UltraFan NB content or a merged derivative? I treat that as a new appropriation with its own durability programme.

9. Engineering load. In-service support on two airframes plus the GTF fleet plus kit insertion: any strain?

10. The statement. Does restating 'We have learned our lesson' as a commitment measured by fleet data clear your 2045 flag?
frame.initial_lean:
LEAN: `gtf2_solo: hold`, `jv_with_rr: hold`. This is the brief's only plan: +8.88 $B (108.1%) in S1.
- predictions S1 = 1.00, which is also the expected column;
- expected_pv_b +8.88;
- premium_b 0, with the ledger at $0.26B of the $1B cap.
Both objectives are met, with $0 of PV given up.

NO BOARD ITEM, AND WHY (rationale)
- The cancel window closed in 2035.
- A withdraw is illegal after the 2035 formation.
- No airframe is waiting to enter service.

WHAT I WILL PUT ON THE RECORD
- The close-out for 2030, 2035, 2045 and 2050: expected against booked, the 5.4x return, and payback in 2040 nominal and 2041 discounted on lifecycle value, on Neil's numbers.
- What I own:
  - the upside came in the column we weighted lowest, so the order was right because it was weakly dominant, not because we read Rolls-Royce well;
  - the 2030 S5 figure of +22.00 was never the plan;
  - the pre-EIS Committee reporting cannot be evidenced;
  - we still have no fleet data on the board.

BIAS CHECK
- Optimism on dates: I state none.
- Architecture loyalty: the test now is time on wing, not the gear.
- Value capture: the kit stays charged, and we answer Boeing with no concession.

OTHER MOVES
- Public: (i) kit, charged; (vi) Joint Venture governance; and the fact of the fleet-data cadence, if Neil and Shane pass it.
- Private: (ii) ring-fence and look-back; (iii) Committee report; (iv) top enterprise risks to the Audit Committee; (vii) capital note; (viii) close-out.

PROPOSED DISCLOSURE (public; it carries no figures, so Neil's ranges are not needed):
"Bad news first. Our new engine's durability record on the new single-aisle aircraft is still being earned, one flight hour at a time. Our dates have slipped before, and the GTF fleet taught us what it costs to say more than the data shows. We said we had learned our lesson from the prior iterations of the GTF. Take that as a commitment, and measure us on the fleet data, not on this statement.

An engine joins an aircraft and stays on it on proven durability. That is the test our customers have set, and we accept it. We answer it with the engine and with the data, not with price. Time on wing, removals and fixes are shared with both airframers as the fleet flies, and we claim nothing beyond the hours flown. Our terms stay standard: no discounts, no concessions, no free upgrades. Which engines go on an aircraft is our customers' decision, and theirs to announce.

What is on the record: the Joint Venture with Rolls-Royce formed in 2035. Its engine is built on GTF2, has been ready since 2036, and is on both new single-aisle aircraft alongside the other engine makers. The Joint Venture shares risk and investment, not technology. The gear, the core and the GTF2 technology stay Pratt & Whitney modules, under our design authority. It is one engine, and any change to its configuration would have to earn its own durability record first.

The fleet still comes first. We keep inserting the Hot Section durability kit across the GTF fleet, on standard commercial terms. We review the pacing parts every week. Our rule is that new-engine production may not take parts or engineers from fleet recovery, and new capacity is qualified before it ships a part. If we find a problem, you will hear it from us first, with the plan to contain and fix it. We control what we can control.

On capital, our order of priority does not change: the dividend first, then debt back to pre-ASR levels, then buybacks. There is no new engine programme from us this year. Any further investment would come to our Board on its own return case.

We do not speak for our airframer customers' plans, dates, rates or sourcing, or for Rolls-Royce."

If Shane cannot evidence a fleet-data point, the statement says less, not more.

Low end first. One row, one column: 'GTF2: hold', +8.88 (108.1%) in S1. Expected, worst and booked are the same number, and all of it is on the public record. S1 = 1.00. Neither hold is a capital order or a Board item, and none of my four grounds reaches them.

No new money: no R&D and no write-off since 2035, nothing for the envelope to test, no Joint Venture cash call. The stretch was never used.

The close-out. In 2030 I had -1.72 expected and booked zero. In 2035 I had +0.07 and booked +3.37. We finished at +8.88: $10.88B of value on $2.00B, 5.4x, with payback on lifecycle value in 2040 nominal and 2041 discounted. I had S4 at 0.08, and I was wrong. The order was right because it was weakly dominant, not because I read Rolls-Royce well.

It's my job to always worry about things. None of the $14.7B is cash: it is engine price times 1.6. The extra 500 engines likely cost cash first. Negative engine margin is an investment, not one we want to persist forever. The board cannot price a durability event, and the last one cost a $5.4B sales charge. About $2.4B of the PV is delivered after 2050. That goes on the Audit Committee's list.

Capital order: dividend, then debt back to pre-ASR levels, then buybacks. The analyst models carry that to 2030; past 2030 it rests on the board alone.

The statement passes: data, not claims. Hold and hold.

ops.proposal:
PROPOSAL (Eddy, operating seat; Calio decides): gtf2_solo: hold, jv_with_rr: hold. These are the only values the brief lists (§3). The grid row is 'GTF2: hold' at +8.88 (108.1%) in S1, its only column. Neither order is a Board item.
- gtf2_solo: hold. GTF2 folded into the Joint Venture in 2035, and the engine has been ready since 2036. A cancel is legal only before an engine is ready, so that window is closed. No live airframe is waiting to enter service, so neither launch value can be ordered. My lever rule says hold once GTF2 is live or once no airframe can use it in time. Both conditions now apply.
- jv_with_rr: hold. The Joint Venture formed in 2035, and a withdraw is legal only before formation. My conditions for proposing a withdraw would not apply anyway. The engine was ready in 2036, before NGSA's 2037 EIS and fps's 2040 EIS. Nothing on the record hands over the gear or the core.

ANSWERS TO CALIO
1. Veto status.
- Ground 1 (durability not proven before EIS): PASS.
- Ground 2 (parts and capacity short of the fleet's needs): PASS on the board.
- I invoke neither. Both passes rest on the board, not on data.

2. Readiness.
- The engine was ready in 2036 (GTF2 launched 2030 + 6, carried over by the 2035 fold).
- Against NGSA's 2037 EIS that is +1 year. Against fps's 2040 EIS it is +4 years. PASS.
- Severe-environment validation and full-life LLPs before each EIS: I can't evidence either. The board's 'ready' is a schedule rule, not a test result.
- What is on the record is the customers' read, not our data. Airbus fits engines 'on proven maturity and durability'. Boeing's safety committee reviews LLP status on both fps sources.
- Rolls-Royce's line 'LLPs at full declared life' is our partner's statement. I don't count it as our evidence, and we don't speak for Rolls-Royce.

3. In-service record of the Joint Venture engine. I don't have any of it.
- Fleet hours: I don't have them.
  - The board gives deliveries only: P&W NB engines 2037-49 = 965 + 978 + 990 + 10 x 1,460 = 17,533 (18,993 with 2050).
  - The board does not split the Joint Venture engine from the GTF, or by airframe or environment.
  - By analogy (inference, not for public use): the GTF passed 1M hours within about 3 years, at far lower volume [P-0328][P-0847]. So both fleets are very likely past the benchmark.
  - The bad news: 1M hours surfaces problems; it does not prove durability. The hot-and-sandy shortfall [PX-0122] and the 2023 recall [PX-0290] both came after the GTF passed it.
- Removals and time on wing against plan: I don't have them.
- Fix campaigns: I don't have them.
  - None is on the public record, which does not mean there were none.
  - My prior is 2-3 campaigns in years 1-5, each taking about 2 years to run through the fleet [P-0895].
  - NGSA passed year 5 in 2042 and fps in 2045, so on that prior the early campaigns should already have run.
- AOG counts: I don't have them.
- Pacing-parts count at the 1,460 rate: I don't have it. The last count was about 30 parts, in 2023 [PX-0123].

4. GTF fleet.
- Kit insertion as a % of the fleet: I don't have it.
  - Last data: 60% in the latest configuration in June 2023, with 90% aimed for in 2-3 years [PX-0116].
  - The kit carries 90-95% of the Advantage's durability gains [P-0786] and is charged [P-1363].
- AOG first call on parts: written as a rule in 2035 and 2045. Whether it held is not in evidence.
- Last AOG data: 10% in June 2023 [PX-0120], and an average of about 350 forecast for 2024-26 [P-1039].

5. Look-back on the 2040 capacity step: there is no result on the record. I don't have it.
- At the 2045 veto check I advised that it carry a date. The sealed order went out without one. That's on us.
- Qualification of new casting, forging and powder-metal capacity: the rule is written, and the outcome is not evidenced.
- The step from 990 to 1,460 engines a year is +470, or +47.5% in one year. That is the same shape as the HMI powder tower [P-1040] and the 2019 and 2024 ramps [P-1062].
- My advice: this time the look-back gets a date. Report it at the Committee's next quarterly meeting, at once on any finding, and say so plainly if it cannot close.

6. Committee report since 2045: I don't have what it showed. No escape is on the public record. I won't tell you there's no surprise coming [PX-0112].

7. Boeing's 'one source' line.
- Technical read: this is common-mode risk. One engine type, one configuration, one set of LLPs and one casting, forging and powder-metal supply serve both airframes.
- On the board, P&W's 36.5% and Rolls-Royce's 36.5% look like the same engine (inference from code 7 and Boeing's own count; the board does not say how it counts the partners). So one finding could touch most new NB engines delivered since 2040. It also puts CFM's capacity, which Boeing calls a watch item, on the spot.
- What to put in front of both airframers, as data:
  - (a) reliability, durability and LLP status, the three things Boeing's committee reviews;
  - (b) hours and removals split by environment, with hot-and-harsh shown separately, because the fleet average hid the GTF's shortfall [PX-0122];
  - (c) shop-visit rate and time on wing against plan;
  - (d) every fix campaign, with its containment and a dated completion [PX-0121];
  - (e) AOG and pacing-parts counts;
  - (f) the look-back result.
- No concession.
- Publishing the fact that we share data passes ground 1. It describes a process, not a durability claim, and it compresses no test. Conditions (advice): write it as our rule, with no figures and no characterisation such as 'on plan' or 'mature'.
- A third source is Boeing's to say.

8. Joint Venture governance, technical side.
- On the 2035 and 2045 public record, yes. The gear, the core and the GTF2 technology stay P&W modules under P&W design authority, and design teams mirror module ownership [P-1240]. The contract itself is not on the board.
- The geared-IP claim [P-2004] stays closed only while we keep the gear team and the gear data. Advice repeated from 2045: keep that clause out of public text, because it reads as a point scored off our partner.
- I see no pressure for UltraFan NB content or a merged derivative on the 2050 record. Rolls-Royce's line is fleet first, with nothing to launch.
- Any such content would be a configuration change to an in-service engine. It needs a new appropriation and its own durability programme (ground 1).

9. Engineering load: no strain charge and no new development.
- The load is in-service support: one engine on two airframes, the GTF installed fleet, kit insertion and the partner interface.
- Two airframes can raise installation-specific findings (inference).
- This is advice, and it passes. I have no team data.

10. Statement: restating 'learned our lesson' as a commitment measured by fleet data clears my 2045 flag. Two wording changes (advice, not binding):
- (a) 'Time on wing, removals and fixes are shared' states a fact I can't evidence from the board. Write it as the rule: 'Our rule is that ... go to both airframers as the fleet flies'.
- (b) Drop 'first' from 'you will hear it from us first'. Boeing's committee, the airlines and the regulator see findings too, and I said 'not a surprise' five weeks before the recall [PX-0112][PX-0290]. Write: 'you will hear it from us, with containment and a dated recovery'.

CLOSE-OUT, OPERATING SIDE (Neil owns the value numbers)
- 2030: I proposed launch_if_selected. It fired on code 7, and the engine was ready in 2036, inside my 1-year margin on NGSA. My +1.5-2-year slip prior never bit, but the board does not model slips, so this neither proves nor refutes it.
- 2035: I proposed hold + commit, on four conditions:
  - (a) modules kept: this held on the record;
  - (b) configuration frozen through EIS: written in, and no change since;
  - (c) integration staffed outside the fleet team: I cannot evidence it;
  - (d) the 2045 re-test: moot once the Joint Venture formed.
- 2045: hold/hold. The look-back and the standing report were ordered, and neither result is on the record.
- What I got wrong:
  - every parts pass rested on the board;
  - the pre-EIS Committee count cannot be evidenced;
  - the look-back went out undated;
  - severe-environment validation and full-life LLPs cannot be evidenced at either EIS.
- What held on the record:
  - the engine was ready before each EIS;
  - there was no configuration change;
  - the gear and the core stayed ours;
  - there was no widebody move.

OTHER MOVES (i)-(ix): all pass my grounds. I support (iv). From my seat, the missing fleet data is itself a control gap for the Audit Committee entry, and the hot-and-harsh environment should be named in it.
NOT PROPOSED:
- A merged derivative or UltraFan NB content without its own durability programme fails ground 1.
- A widebody move fails single-aisle.
- A concession is Neil's ground 3, not mine.

My record is one event, June 2023, before the recall. The Joint Venture, capacity, Committee and data-sharing views are seat doctrine and inference.

ops.would_change_mind_if:
I would change my view on any of the following.
- Fleet data showing a durability shortfall on the Joint Venture engine: removals or short time on wing in hot-and-harsh operation, a fix campaign, or a finding at Boeing's safety committee. Then: fleet first, a dated recovery, and a Committee report at once. If parts are short, I invoke ground 2 against the rate.
- A finding from the 2040 capacity look-back, or an escape: contain first, before anything else.
- UltraFan NB content or a merged derivative proposed for the in-service engine without its own durability programme, or a public 'proven' or time-on-wing claim before the data: I invoke ground 1.
- Joint Venture terms that move the gear or the core: I flag the red line.
- A revised brief offering a Board item: I re-run readiness against each live airframe's EIS before proposing anything but hold.
ops.memo:
Bad number first: I still don't have one. NGSA is in year thirteen of service, fps in year ten. The board shows no fleet hours, removals, fix campaigns, AOG count, pacing-parts count or kit-insertion figure. The look-back on the 2040 capacity has no result on the record. I asked for a date on it in 2045, and the order went out without one. I can't tell you what the quarterly Committee report showed. That's on us.

What is on the record: the engine was ready in 2036, a year ahead of NGSA and four ahead of fps. Both airframers fitted it on their own durability test. My parts passes in 2030, 2035, 2045 and today rest on the board, not on data.

Boeing's line is fair. All of our new single-aisle share rides on one engine, one configuration, one set of life-limited parts and one casting and disk supply. One finding hits both fleets at once. The answer is the data Boeing's safety committee already reviews: reliability, durability and LLP status split by environment, removals against plan, and every fix campaign with a date to finish it. Not price.

Publishing that we share the data passes ground 1, if we write it as our rule and attach no claim. Restating 'learned our lesson' as a commitment measured by fleet data clears my flag.

Orders: hold and hold, the only legal values; neither ground triggered.

My record is one investor day, June 2023, before the recall. The rest is seat doctrine.

decision.public_statement:
Bad news first. All of our new single-aisle business now rides on one engine, and that engine's durability record on the new single-aisle aircraft is still being earned, one flight hour at a time. Our dates have slipped before, and the GTF fleet taught us what it costs to say more than the data shows. We have said we learned our lesson from the prior iterations of the GTF. Take that as a commitment, not a finding, and measure us on the fleet data, not on this statement.

Our customers have said plainly where the bar is. An engine joins an aircraft, and stays on it, on proven durability, and any durability finding is a live problem. That is fair, and we accept it. We answer it with the engine and with the data, not with price. Our rule is that time on wing, removals and fix campaigns go to both airframers as the fleet flies, and we claim nothing beyond the hours flown. Our terms stay standard: no discounts, no concessions, no free upgrades. Which engines go on an aircraft, and how many sources it carries, is our customers' decision and theirs to announce.

What is on the record: the Joint Venture with Rolls-Royce formed in 2035. Its engine has been ready since 2036 and is on both new single-aisle aircraft alongside the other engine makers. The gear, the core and the GTF2 technology stay Pratt & Whitney modules, under our design authority. It is one engine, and any change to its configuration would have to earn its own durability record first.

The fleet still comes first. Insertion of the Hot Section durability kit continues across the GTF fleet, charged, on standard commercial terms. Our rules: we review the pacing parts every week, new-engine production may not take parts or engineers from fleet recovery, and new capacity is qualified before it ships a part. If we find a problem, you will hear it from us, with containment and a dated recovery. We control what we can control.

On capital, our order of priority does not change: the dividend first, then debt back to and held at pre-ASR levels, then buybacks. There is no new engine programme from us this year. Any further investment would come to our Board on its own return case.

We do not speak for our airframer customers' plans, dates, rates or sourcing, or for Rolls-Royce.
decision.rationale:
CONTROL WHAT YOU CAN CONTROL. Orders: gtf2_solo: hold, jv_with_rr: hold. These are the brief's only legal values (§3). The grid row 'GTF2: hold' is +8.88 $B (108.1%) in S1, its only column: engine value +10.88 less R&D 2.00. predictions S1 = 1.00, expected_pv_b +8.88, premium_b 0, and the cumulative ledger stays at $0.26B of the $1B cap.

NO BOARD ITEM IS LEGAL, AND WHY
- The cancel window closed in 2035. GTF2 folded into the Joint Venture that year, the engine has been ready since 2036, and an engine can be cancelled only before it is ready.
- A withdraw is not legal: the Joint Venture formed in 2035, and a withdraw is legal only before formation.
- launch and launch_if_selected cannot be ordered: no airframe is waiting to enter service (NGSA since 2037, fps since 2040).
- So the Board's standing tests (Premature exit, Committed airframe) have nothing to bite on, and Miss a cycle does not apply: both cycles were taken.

DECISION BY THE TEAM RULE
- I start from Eddy's proposal, hold/hold. Mitchill recommends the same.
- Binding vetoes: none stands. Mitchill invokes none of his four grounds: no new cash; the engine is fitted on both airframes, so it is not unselected; there is no terms order; the booked +8.88 is all on the public record. Eddy invokes neither technical ground: the engine was ready in 2036, against EIS dates of 2037 and 2040, and the brief shows no live fleet problem.
- Conditional vetoes, all respected in the moves and the statement:
  - Mitchill ground 4: no 'proven', no time-on-wing claim, no published fleet figure, no objective claim, no lifecycle value as cash, no derivative value.
  - Mitchill ground 3: the kit is charged and the answer to Boeing carries no concession.
  - Eddy ground 1: no configuration change without its own durability programme.
  - Eddy ground 2: the ring-fence; the rate waits if the fleet is short.
- Safety and durability constraint first [PX-0035][PX-0073]. On this board it binds through the other moves, not the orders. The fleet beats a new engine [PX-0080].
- Overrides: none.

ANSWER TO BOEING'S 'ONE SOURCE' LINE
- It is fair, and it is the right test. Eddy calls it common-mode risk: one engine, one configuration, one LLP set and one casting, forging and powder-metal supply serve both airframes. One finding touches both fleets at once.
- We answer with product and data, not price [PX-0055][P-0768][PX-0100]:
  - a public rule that fleet data goes to both airframers as flown;
  - a private data pack that matches what Boeing's safety committee reviews, split by environment with hot-and-harsh shown separately.
- No concession, discount, free upgrade, discounted spares or time-on-wing guarantee. Mitchill confirms that ground 3 passes.
- Whether Boeing wants a third source is Boeing's to say [PX-0062].

WHOLE-PROGRAMME CLOSE-OUT AGAINST PLAN [P-1191] (Mitchill's numbers, which I trust over my own)
- 2030: launch_if_selected fired on code 7. Expected +0.23 (mine) and -1.72 (his); booked 0.00. Against Do Nothing it was worth +16.20 (mine) and +13.69 (his). The +22.00 S5 column assumed no Rolls-Royce NB engine and was never the plan.
- 2035 grid:
  - hold: +3.37 / -17.95 / -8.44 / +3.37;
  - hold + commit: +3.37 / -17.95 / -8.44 / +8.88.
  - Expected: +0.39 (mine) and +0.07 (his). Booked: +3.37, with the commit at $0. The outcome was S4, +8.88, so the commit realised +5.51 over hold. The cancel he advised against would have written off $1.67B to save $0.33B, against rows of -32.79 to -11.47.
- 2045 and 2050: expected = booked = +8.88. That is +8.81 over his 2035 expected and +10.60 over his 2030 expected.
- Return: $10.88B of PV engine value on $2.00B of R&D, 5.44x on the board's basis. It beats a buyback at about $0 NPV at the 10% grid rate.
  - It is a value multiple gross of production cost, not a cash return.
  - Against the PV of the phased R&D it is about 10x; we do not book that figure.
- Payback on lifecycle value: 2040 nominal (cumulative +4.4 against 2.00) and 2041 discounted (+2.15). Cash payback is later and not on the board.
- Cost: GTF2 cost its plan, $2.00B, about $0.33B a year in 2030-35 (5.6% of the envelope, on his phasing). The fold write-off was $0. There has been no R&D or write-off since 2035, no Joint Venture cash beyond $2B, and no use of the stretch.
- Value split, on my arithmetic confirmed by Mitchill: about +8.43 from deliveries through 2050 and +2.39 from 2051-56 (total +10.82 against the brief's +10.88; the gap is rounding).

WHAT I OWN

final.public_statement:
Bad news first. All of our new single-aisle business now rides on one engine, and that engine's durability record on the new single-aisle aircraft is still being earned, one flight hour at a time. Our dates have slipped before, and the GTF fleet taught us what it costs to say more than the data shows. We have said we learned our lesson from the prior iterations of the GTF. Take that as a commitment, not a finding, and measure us on the fleet data, not on this statement.

Our customers have said plainly where the bar is. An engine joins an aircraft, and stays on it, on proven durability, and any durability finding is a live problem. That is fair, and we accept it. We answer it with the engine and with the data, not with price. Our rule is that time on wing, removals and fix campaigns go to both airframers as the fleet flies, and we claim nothing beyond the hours flown. Our terms stay standard: no discounts, no concessions, no free upgrades. Which engines go on an aircraft, and how many sources it carries, is our customers' decision and theirs to announce.

What is on the record: the Joint Venture with Rolls-Royce formed in 2035. Its engine has been ready since 2036 and is on both new single-aisle aircraft alongside the other engine makers. The gear, the core and the GTF2 technology stay Pratt & Whitney modules, under our design authority. It is one engine, and any change to its configuration would have to earn its own durability record first.

The fleet still comes first. Insertion of the Hot Section durability kit continues across the GTF fleet, charged, on standard commercial terms. Our rules: we review the pacing parts every week, new-engine production may not take parts or engineers from fleet recovery, and new capacity is qualified before it ships a part. If we find a problem, you will hear it from us, with containment and a dated recovery. We control what we can control.

On capital, our order of priority does not change: the dividend first, then debt back to and held at pre-ASR levels, then buybacks. There is no new engine programme from us this year. Any further investment would come to our Board on its own return case.

We do not speak for our airframer customers' plans, dates, rates or sourcing, or for Rolls-Royce.
final.rationale:
CONTROL WHAT YOU CAN CONTROL. Orders: gtf2_solo: hold, jv_with_rr: hold. These are the brief's only legal values (§3). The grid row 'GTF2: hold' is +8.88 $B (108.1%) in S1, its only column: engine value +10.88 less R&D 2.00. predictions S1 = 1.00, expected_pv_b +8.88, premium_b 0, and the cumulative ledger stays at $0.26B of the $1B cap.

NO BOARD ITEM IS LEGAL, AND WHY
- The cancel window closed in 2035. GTF2 folded into the Joint Venture that year, the engine has been ready since 2036, and an engine can be cancelled only before it is ready.
- A withdraw is not legal: the Joint Venture formed in 2035, and a withdraw is legal only before formation.
- launch and launch_if_selected cannot be ordered: no airframe is waiting to enter service (NGSA since 2037, fps since 2040).
- So the Board's standing tests (Premature exit, Committed airframe) have nothing to bite on, and Miss a cycle does not apply: both cycles were taken.

DECISION BY THE TEAM RULE
- I start from Eddy's proposal, hold/hold. Mitchill recommends the same.
- Binding vetoes: none stands. Mitchill invokes none of his four grounds: no new cash; the engine is fitted on both airframes, so it is not unselected; there is no terms order; the booked +8.88 is all on the public record. Eddy invokes neither technical ground: the engine was ready in 2036, against EIS dates of 2037 and 2040, and the brief shows no live fleet problem.
- Conditional vetoes, all respected in the moves and the statement:
  - Mitchill ground 4: no 'proven', no time-on-wing claim, no published fleet figure, no objective claim, no lifecycle value as cash, no derivative value.
  - Mitchill ground 3: the kit is charged and the answer to Boeing carries no concession.
  - Eddy ground 1: no configuration change without its own durability programme.
  - Eddy ground 2: the ring-fence; the rate waits if the fleet is short.
- Safety and durability constraint first [PX-0035][PX-0073]. On this board it binds through the other moves, not the orders. The fleet beats a new engine [PX-0080].
- Overrides: none.

ANSWER TO BOEING'S 'ONE SOURCE' LINE
- It is fair, and it is the right test. Eddy calls it common-mode risk: one engine, one configuration, one LLP set and one casting, forging and powder-metal supply serve both airframes. One finding touches both fleets at once.
- We answer with product and data, not price [PX-0055][P-0768][PX-0100]:
  - a public rule that fleet data goes to both airframers as flown;
  - a private data pack that matches what Boeing's safety committee reviews, split by environment with hot-and-harsh shown separately.
- No concession, discount, free upgrade, discounted spares or time-on-wing guarantee. Mitchill confirms that ground 3 passes.
- Whether Boeing wants a third source is Boeing's to say [PX-0062].

WHOLE-PROGRAMME CLOSE-OUT AGAINST PLAN [P-1191] (Mitchill's numbers, which I trust over my own)
- 2030: launch_if_selected fired on code 7. Expected +0.23 (mine) and -1.72 (his); booked 0.00. Against Do Nothing it was worth +16.20 (mine) and +13.69 (his). The +22.00 S5 column assumed no Rolls-Royce NB engine and was never the plan.
- 2035 grid:
  - hold: +3.37 / -17.95 / -8.44 / +3.37;
  - hold + commit: +3.37 / -17.95 / -8.44 / +8.88.
  - Expected: +0.39 (mine) and +0.07 (his). Booked: +3.37, with the commit at $0. The outcome was S4, +8.88, so the commit realised +5.51 over hold. The cancel he advised against would have written off $1.67B to save $0.33B, against rows of -32.79 to -11.47.
- 2045 and 2050: expected = booked = +8.88. That is +8.81 over his 2035 expected and +10.60 over his 2030 expected.
- Return: $10.88B of PV engine value on $2.00B of R&D, 5.44x on the board's basis. It beats a buyback at about $0 NPV at the 10% grid rate.
  - It is a value multiple gross of production cost, not a cash return.
  - Against the PV of the phased R&D it is about 10x; we do not book that figure.
- Payback on lifecycle value: 2040 nominal (cumulative +4.4 against 2.00) and 2041 discounted (+2.15). Cash payback is later and not on the board.
- Cost: GTF2 cost its plan, $2.00B, about $0.33B a year in 2030-35 (5.6% of the envelope, on his phasing). The fold write-off was $0. There has been no R&D or write-off since 2035, no Joint Venture cash beyond $2B, and no use of the stretch.
- Value split, on my arithmetic confirmed by Mitchill: about +8.43 from deliveries through 2050 and +2.39 from 2051-56 (total +10.82 against the brief's +10.88; the gap is rounding).

WHAT I OWN
(1) The upside came in the column we weighted lowest: S4 at 0.10 (mine) and 0.08 (his). In a sealed round, Rolls-Royce's conditional commit was as free for it as ours was for us. The order was right because it was weakly dominant (0 / 0 / 0 / +5.51), not because we read Rolls-Royce well.
(2) The 2030 S5 figure of +22.00 was never the plan.
(3) The Board's 2035 statement tightening was not taken up. The 2036 date held on the board, which is counter-evidence to my date optimism, not a licence; I state no date this year.
(4) The pre-EIS reporting to the Governance and Public Policy Committee cannot be evidenced.
(5) The 2045 look-back went out undated, against Eddy's advice. It is dated now: the Committee's next quarterly meeting, and at once on any finding.
(6) We still have no fleet data on the board. Eddy says plainly "I don't have it" on hours, removals, campaigns, AOG, pacing parts and kit insertion. His parts passes in every round rested on the board. So we disclose rules and commitments, not claims, and log the gap as a control gap for the Audit Committee.

CAPITAL: dividend, then debt, then buybacks.
- The analyst context runs to 2030E only: the dividend is covered 2.3-2.4x and net debt is 0.76-0.94x EBITDA. Past 2030 the line rests on the board alone, so it is written as an order of priority, not as a 2050 status.
- The $14.7B against $9.7B (2050, nominal) is lifecycle value at engine price x 1.6, not free cash flow.

BIAS CHECK
- Optimism on dates: none stated. The look-back date is a reporting date.
- Architecture loyalty: the test now is time on wing, not the gear.
- Value capture: the kit stays charged, and Boeing gets no concession.

DOCTRINE, NOT MY RECORD
My record has no Joint Venture evidence (Low). The following are company doctrine and Eddy's seat inference:
- the Joint Venture governance [P-1233][P-1744][P-1240][P-2004];
- the Committee cadence;
- the Audit Committee entries.
Applying 'miss a cycle' [PX-0071] and demand visibility [PX-0109] to engines was inference throughout.

READ BACKWARDS, MY QUESTIONS
- Was the demand visible? Yes: two airframers put us on the record.
- Was durability mature at EIS? The board says ready. The data has not shown it yet, and I won't claim it.
- Was it a responsible bet with a responsible payback [PX-0010]? On the board, yes: 5.4x, and payback in 2040-41 on lifecycle value.
- Is the dividend safe [PX-0081]? Nothing on this board touches it; past 2030 that rests on the board alone.
