recommendations.text:
Defend the widebody core inside the existing budget, and hold both widebody orders in this last round. Continue Trent time on wing as an unpriced other move: HP turbine blades on the Trent 1000 and Trent 7000, life-limited-part life extension, and Trent XWB shop-visit cost down.

Airbus says it will take a further A350 step only when 'the technology, the engine and the business case are all ready'. Our part is to keep the Trent XWB ready commercially and technically, on standard terms, without a programme order. We power the A350 alone, so watch that exposure.

If a Re-engine goes on the record this round, record in `rationale` how we would answer it after the game: an airframe on the record first, the strain shown, and the case made on its own return. We are a long-term business with very long investment cycles. Long-term widebody presence is earned through the fleet we have.

Funding discipline. McCabe should keep reporting each quarter on our share of narrowbody ramp and early-unit costs, shared with Pratt & Whitney, against her base of about $1.9-4.3B and her reasonable worst case of about $7.5B ($9B if we carry a retrofit alone). The report should also cover the net LTSA balance, time on wing and any onerous-contract provision.

Our order holds: the balance sheet first, then the 30-40% dividend, then investment and further distributions. If the ramp or a fleet fix runs over, buybacks give way first, as in 2015, and a fleet fix is never re-phased for cash. Any need for equity, leverage above about 1.5x or borrowing for distributions comes to the board before it arises. Gross R&D stays broadly flat.

frame.question:
So, 2050. This is the last round. There is nothing left to launch on the narrowbody, and the question is cash and quality of earnings, not share [RX-0054].

Where we stand:
- The Joint Venture formed in 2035. Its engine has been ready since 2036, on NGSA since 2037 and on fps since 2040.
- We hold 36.5% of narrowbody engines, 1,460 a year: about 17,533 in our share by end-2049 and 18,993 by end-2050 (brief year table).
- Widebody share is 55.2% in 2050 (58.0% in S3).
- Hold is worth +32.35 / +32.35 / +32.70 in S1-S3.

The question has three parts.
(1) Does the installed fleet turn into durable, profitable aftermarket cash?
- Boeing now says in public that the Joint Venture engine is one of exactly two fps sources, and that any durability finding would make it want a third.
- P&W says the engine's durability record is 'still being earned'.
- So our narrowbody position rests on durability in service, not on a next programme.
- The Trent 1000 is the movie I have seen before [RX-0087, RX-0114].
(2) Does any widebody spend earn its keep beside the narrowbody in the last round? Frankly, no.
- The Trent 1000 upgrade is -6.72 / -6.72 / -6.62 against hold, and UltraFan WB is -9.00 / -8.67 / -8.32.
- Each loses more than its own bill in every column, with a permanent $5B of strain stacked on it.
(3) Is the partnership aligned on terms that protect our cash? The governance note is due now. It covers:
- design authority;
- data on the hot section and life-limited parts;
- retrofit liability;
- work and revenue share against equal 36.5% shares;
- our cash staying within the $4B share.

'I worry about tomorrow's financials' [RX-0125]. We close the game on cash, not on a launch.

ops.memo:
The fleet comes first. The Joint Venture engine has been ready since 2036: on NGSA since 2037 and fps since 2040, 1,460 engines a year in our share, 17,533 by end-2049. No readiness test applies to this round's orders, and no Civil ground arises at hold.

Durability: the record shows no in-service event, and I claim nothing beyond it. What we can't see is the hot section and the life-limited parts. P&W holds design authority there and is still inserting its Hot Section kit across the GTF fleet. Boeing has told us the stakes: our engine is one of two fps sources. The governance note must give us that data in proportion to the risk we carry, and the Trent 1000 rule: Committee first, inspection intervals and a spare-engine pool, the design authority's kit through the joint partner shops, anything new waits.

Support: the 2037-40 cohorts are 4,393 engines in our share. The board shows no shortfall. My watch items are shop induction slots, life-limited-part and hot-section spares, and spare engines for severe-environment operators, ahead of the first wave.

Widebody: 55.2% in 2050, 58.0% in S3, above the line. I'd normally back the upgrade, but it's -6.72, and -1.72 even without the strain. UltraFan WB would be ready in 2056, a year after a 2050 Re-engine's EIS. Hold both; time on wing inside the budget does the job.

Statement clean. Every field at hold.

We're absolutely focused on keeping our engines flying and earning for as long as possible.

other_moves.move: Fleet first on the Joint Venture engine in service
other_moves.detail: The Joint Venture engine is in service on NGSA and fps. Rolls-Royce puts the installed fleet first: durability in service, life-limited parts at full declared life, and support through the joint partner-shop network. If durability bites, the fleet is fixed first and anything new waits. We report what the fleet data shows and claim nothing beyond it. No dates, no retrofit or kit timing, and no Joint Venture terms beyond the public record.

other_moves.move: Quarterly fleet report to the Safety, Energy Transition & Tech Committee (Watson)
Joint Venture governance note to the Board, delivered now (Watson and McCabe)
other_moves.detail:
The note the Board asked for before 2050. Company doctrine (the IAE lesson) and inference: my record is Low on Joint Venture terms.
OPERATING SIDE (Watson):
(1) Design authority, stated plainly. On the record P&W holds the gear, the core and GTF2 as its modules under its design authority. It is one engine and one support chain. In this engine we bring risk, investment and the support network. We hold no module design authority.
(2) Our technology role. UltraFan stays ours and feeds the Trent fleet. 'We are actually bringing a technology' [RX-0072] belongs to a later engine under our own design authority, not this one.
(3) Data. Hot-section, life-limited-part and severe-environment fleet data through the joint support agreement, in proportion to our equal 36.5% share of the risk. Without it Watson cannot report durability to the Committee beyond the public record.
(4) Support network. Our Singapore-model partner shops plus P&W's in-service shops. Induction slots, spares and a spare-engine pool planned jointly ahead of the 2037-40 wave. Any kit goes in at shop visit through these shops.
MONEY SIDE (McCabe):
(5) Work share and revenue share at 36.5% each, matching the equal engine shares. The board credits our 1,460 engines a year at full value, which matches our cash only at about half the content and revenue of each Joint Venture engine. Each 10 points of content below half takes about $7.7B off the narrowbody value: at 40% content engine value is about +30.3 and hold about +24.6; at 30%, about +22.6 and +16.9. Service revenue counts as much as build work share.
(6) Retrofit liability. Cost follows design authority, or we get a joint say in the fix. Planning figure: half a Trent 1000-type bill, about £1.1bn; worst case about £2.2bn. That anchor comes from a smaller widebody fleet, so it is a planning figure, not a ceiling. Any finding comes to the Board with a fresh number before anything is public.
(7) Cash. Our money stays within the $4B share. No Rolls-Royce money beyond it without the Board.
(8) Configuration. Any UltraFan NB content or merged derivative is a new programme: it comes to the Board on its own return case and its own durability record, as P&W's public terms also require.
(9) Alignment. Who books the service contracts on our 36.5% is to be settled in the note, so the narrowbody float is proven, not assumed. We left IAE for want of alignment; we will not drift there again.

other_moves.move: Funding discipline and quarterly report to the Board (McCabe)
other_moves.detail:
Our share of narrowbody ramp and early-unit costs, shared with P&W, held at the top of the base range until actuals exist: about $4.3B (£3.1bn) against a base of about $1.9-4.3B (£1.4-3.1bn). Reasonable worst case about $7.5B (£5.5bn) with a retrofit shared 50/50, or about $9B (£6.7bn) if we carry a retrofit alone. The window rolls forward to the first shop-visit wave from the 2037-40 cohorts.
Also each quarter: the net LTSA balance (no narrowbody float booked until the governance note settles who holds the service contracts), time on wing (no upside booked before it is delivered), and any onerous-contract provision, booked plainly if a Joint Venture contract turns loss-making.
Order: the balance sheet, then the 30-40% dividend, then investment and further distributions. If the ramp or a fleet fix runs over, buybacks give way first, and a fleet fix is never re-phased for cash. No equity, leverage below about 1.5x, no borrowing for distributions. Gross R&D stays broadly flat. No balance-sheet trigger stands.

other_moves.move: Trent time on wing and fleet support inside the existing budget (Watson)
other_moves.detail: Longer-life HP turbine blades on the Trent 1000 and Trent 7000, life extension for life-limited parts, UltraFan technology fed into the Trent fleet, and Trent XWB shop-visit cost down. Funded inside the existing fleet budget. This is not the `t1000_upgrade` order and not a new programme, and it carries no strain. We keep the Trent XWB ready commercially and technically for the A350 family on standard terms, and watch our sole-source exposure there. No dates disclosed.

other_moves.move: Commercial terms with Airbus and Boeing
other_moves.detail: Standard commercial terms with both airframers on NGSA, fps and the widebody fleets: value remunerated, win-win. No launch-style concession, discount or free upgrade to hold a position. Every new contract goes through the Investment Committee [RX-0081, RX-0097, R-1582]. We do not speak for any airframer's dates or rates.

decision.public_statement: So, plainly. The Joint Venture with Pratt & Whitney formed in 2035, and its engine is in service on both new narrowbodies. Now it has to earn its keep in the fleet. The fleet comes first: durability in service, life-limited parts at full life, and support through the joint partner-shop network. We will report what the fleet shows, and claim nothing more. If anything has to give, we fix the fleet first and anything new waits. Widebody is our core: no new widebody programme beside the narrowbody, and Trent time on wing keeps improving. We price for value, not share, on standard commercial terms with both airframers. Frankly, there is nothing to launch this year. We won't do anything not profitable. I will say that categorically.
decision.rationale:
DECISION
Every field is at hold. This is my framing proposal, unchanged, and both memos recommend it:
- `ultrafan_nb_solo: hold`
- `jv_with_pw: hold`
- `ultrafan_wb: hold`
- `t1000_upgrade: hold`
None of these is a Board item. Do Nothing on widebody (Trent only) is right because no airframe can use a new widebody engine in time, and neither widebody order earns its bill [RX-0058].

final.public_statement: So, plainly. The Joint Venture with Pratt & Whitney formed in 2035, and its engine is in service on both new narrowbodies. Now it has to earn its keep in the fleet. The fleet comes first: durability in service, life-limited parts at full life, and support through the joint partner-shop network. We will report what the fleet shows, and claim nothing more. If anything has to give, we fix the fleet first and anything new waits. Widebody is our core: no new widebody programme beside the narrowbody, and Trent time on wing keeps improving. We price for value, not share, on standard commercial terms with both airframers. Frankly, there is nothing to launch this year. We won't do anything not profitable. I will say that categorically.
final.rationale:
DECISION
Every field is at hold. This is my framing proposal, unchanged, and both memos recommend it:
- `ultrafan_nb_solo: hold`
- `jv_with_pw: hold`
- `ultrafan_wb: hold`
- `t1000_upgrade: hold`
None of these is a Board item. Do Nothing on widebody (Trent only) is right because no airframe can use a new widebody engine in time, and neither widebody order earns its bill [RX-0058].

GRID (brief rows, S1 / S2 / S3), weights 0.80 / 0.12 / 0.08
- "UltraFan NB: hold": +32.35 / +32.35 / +32.70. Expected +32.38 (+32.385 at the Board's 0.80 / 0.10 / 0.10, +32.42 at McCabe's stress 0.60 / 0.20 / 0.20). Worst column +32.35. Best row in every column.
- "UltraFan NB: hold + T1000 upgrade": +25.63 / +25.63 / +26.08. Against hold: -6.72 / -6.72 / -6.62, so -6.71 weighted. Worst -6.72, 3.4x its $2B bill. Without the $5B strain it is still -1.72 / -1.72 / -1.62. It counts only from 2053, so 2050 widebody share does not move.
- "UltraFan NB: hold + UltraFan WB": +23.35 / +23.68 / +24.38. Against hold: -9.00 / -8.67 / -8.32, so -8.91 weighted (-8.90 at the Board's weights). Worst -9.00, 2.25x its $4B bill. Without the strain it is -4.00 / -3.67 / -3.32. It would be ready in 2056, a year after a 2050 Re-engine's 2055 EIS.
- Upgrade plus UltraFan WB together: not allowed (exclusive).
The verdict does not depend on the weights: hold is best in every column.

VETO CHECKS
- McCabe: she withholds her co-signature on both `t1000_upgrade: launch` and `ultrafan_wb: launch`, on hurdle and downside. These are binding, and I give neither order. No balance-sheet veto arises: no new money, debt unchanged, no equity, leverage well below about 1.5x.
- Watson: no Civil veto at hold. Nothing is compressed, no early date is disclosed, and no narrowbody launch, trigger or commit needs a support plan. He cleared the draft statement. The one line I added ('We will report what the fleet shows, and claim nothing more') has no date, no terms and no claim of RR module content, so it stays inside his test. He keeps his re-check of the final text.
- No revision is needed. `overrides` is empty.

RED LINES (checked before return)
- McCabe's note that an UltraFan WB launch would also breach 'no UltraFan launch without a programme that can fly it'. Confirmed and struck: no UltraFan WB launch is ordered.
- Overlap: no UltraFan is in development, so the upgrade rule is not engaged. No Solo stands, so the UltraFan WB-beside-Solo rule is not engaged.
- Strain: none ordered. Control's strain line stays at $0.
- Disclosure: no new programme, retrofit, kit or growth-engine date. Nothing on Re-engines or any airframer's dates or rates. No Joint Venture terms beyond the record. No claim of RR module technology in the in-service engine.
- Cancel: none is open, and none is needed. No orphan programme stands.
No red-line flag is left unresolved.

PREMIUM: $0, item by item. No doctrine-favoured order is kept against the grid.

WHAT THE GRID DOES NOT SHOW
1. Content per engine. McCabe's rebuild puts about +38.6 of our +38.07 engine value in narrowbody and about -0.5 in widebody. The board credits our 1,460 engines a year at full value, which matches our cash only at about half the content and revenue of each Joint Venture engine. Each 10 points below half costs about $7.7B. So work share and revenue share at 36.5% each heads the governance note.
2. Durability. P&W says the record is 'still being earned' and is still inserting its Hot Section kit across the GTF fleet. Boeing says that if the Joint Venture engine stumbles, the fps is back on CFM alone. The share risk and the retrofit bill sit off the board. We cannot see the hot-section or life-limited-part data, so getting it is the note's first operating ask. Actually, I've seen this movie before [RX-0087]: the Trent 1000 is the precedent we will not repeat.

IF A RE-ENGINE GOES ON THE RECORD THIS ROUND (orders are sealed, so this is the answer after the game)
- The airframe goes on the record first. For UltraFan WB, that means an A350 Re-engine on the record, or a 787 Re-engine on which Boeing has named UltraFan.
- The strain is shown: $5B, permanent, beside the Joint Venture.
- The case is made on its own return against hold, inside the caps ($1B for UltraFan WB).
- Readiness is Watson's: UltraFan WB at launch + 6 against the Re-engine's EIS. On this brief, 2056 misses a 2050 Re-engine's 2055 EIS by a year.
- Until then, we defend the widebody through the fleet we have: Trent XWB time on wing and shop-visit cost, on standard terms.

RECORD AND DOCTRINE
- From my record: the cash framing, 'won't do anything not profitable', choices not options.
- Company doctrine and my colleagues' inference, because my record is Low there: the Joint Venture governance asks (the IAE lesson). The cash figures are McCabe's; the readiness and support views are Watson's.
